newsitem.title: KENYA: Kenya counts cost as Mombasa violence wanes.
newsitem.headline: Kenya counts cost as Mombasa violence wanes.

text.p: An explosion of violence on Kenya's tourist coast appeared to be waning on Tuesday but it has cost at least 35 lives and done more damage to the East African country's battered image.
Witnesses on Tuesday reported two incidents overnight in the coast region, saying three houses were set on fire overnight at Ntopanga and in a skirmish at Kiembeni some people were wounded.

President Daniel arap Moi's government and the opposition, heading for elections which threaten to bring more trouble, blamed each other for six days of brutal attacks around the Indian Ocean port of Mombasa.
Foreign tourists who flock to the coast's glorious beaches and busy nightlife were not targets and by Tuesday none had been reported injured.
But extreme acts of violence, including mutilations and the murders of at least nine police officers, were committed within sight of the holiday havens which are Kenya's top foreign currency earner.
Germany, Belgium, Italy and Britain all told their tourists to be extra careful and avoid trouble-spots.
"We are enjoying ourselves and I have not been affected but I am fully aware through newspapers and television," said Bob Barrett, a British tourist from Staffordshire.
"You must ask what is wrong with the government here, why they allow this to continue."
A Pakistani tourist said she was coming from Mombasa early on Sunday when she saw flames from burning houses and small children huddled by the roadside.
"I am enjoying but my heart wonders how they are doing because I saw them in extreme trouble," she said.
Kenyan tourist officials report few cancellations so far but say any incident involving a foreign visitor would be a disaster for the industry, which earned $465 million in 1996.
More than half of last year's 770,000 tourists -- itself a declining figure -- headed for the beaches south and north of Mombasa.

Even before Mombasa, Kenya's image had taken a battering because of widely publicised pre-election violence and official corruption which led the International Monetary Fund and World Bank to shelve loans.
The shilling dropped to a historic official low against the dollar on Monday before firming slightly.
By Tuesday hopes were rising that the worst of the violence was over and Mombasa police claimed "peace has been restored".

No killings were reported during the day on Monday although two missing policemen were found dead in a mortuary and a priest and a civilian were slashed to death with machetes during the previous night.
Police said arrests in their joint security operation with the army and navy had risen to 102 on Monday with several political activists among them.
A Mombasa leader of the unregistered opposition party Safina was one of them and his colleagues said he had been tortured in custody.

Mombasa police chief Francis Gichuki confirmed the arrest of a well-known local supporter of Moi's ruling Kenya African National Union (KANU). Sixteen suspects appeared in court accused of possessing weapons such as bows and weapons.
Moi, aged 73 and in power since 1978, has yet to name the date for polls this year where he will seek another -- and legally a final -- five-year term.
The divided but numerous opponents ranged him against have stepped up their campaign for sweeping political and constitutional reforms, saying fair elections are impossible under the existing rules.
They called for more protest rallies on August 23 after earlier demonstrations in which at least 12 people have died.

Moi has blamed the opposition for fanning tribal hatred in Mombasa. But the pro-reform umbrella group and 14 opposition members of parliament replied on Monday that KANU hardliners were stoking the violence to block compromise before the polls.
